title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A at Mendoza College of Business - University of Notre Dame on September 29, 2023
summary: In a Q&A with Notre Dame students, Pabrai explains why compounders should be held even when they look 20-30% overvalued (sell only when egregious), tells the story of Buffett rejecting his 1999 job request and the birth of Pabrai Investment Funds, and argues for a 'Swiss Army Knife' approach using Buffett's yen-financed Japanese trading company bet as an example. He gives students a hack for finding compounders through their own spending, extols shameless cloning with the Chipotle, GM-to-Fiat Chrysler and NVR-homebuilder examples, discusses Munger's psychology models and the reciprocation tendency, bridge, and Dakshana's scaling limits.

ideas.idea: Do not sell a great compounder when it is 20-30% overvalued; sell only when overvaluation is egregious, which becomes obvious when it happens.
ideas.detail: Great compounders are rare and intrinsic value is error-prone: Amazon always looked optically overvalued because reinvestment depressed earnings and no one could see AWS before it surfaced. Microsoft's only clear sell point in 40 years was around 2000 at a $600 billion valuation. Amazon at $1.3 trillion would not bother him at $2-2.5 trillion.

ideas.idea: Adopt a founder's mindset: a founder would not sell for 20-30% above his estimate of value but would happily sell at 500%.
ideas.detail: Giving a business rope means you may sell a 30x or 50x winner 20-30% below its peak when it goes into decline, but 'there are far worse tragedies'; the downside of getting off a great runway is much worse.

ideas.idea: He started Pabrai Investment Funds in 1999 as 'plan B' after Buffett turned down his letter asking to work for him for free.
ideas.detail: With a liquid net worth north of $10 million he wrote Buffett in early 1999; Buffett replied within a week that he works alone and 'I am not the answer'. Eight or nine YPO friends gave him $100,000 each; after being up ~70% in the first year and reaching $2.5 million in 2000 he decided to treat it as a real business.

ideas.idea: Keep a 'Swiss Army Knife' approach: compounders are plan A, but net-nets, merger arbitrage, convertibles and special situations are useful plans B, C and D while you wait.
ideas.detail: Buffett's 2023 letter said 12 decisions in 58 years created 80-90% of Berkshire's value out of more than 300 stocks bought, roughly one great decision every five years, so even Buffett needs other tools.

ideas.idea: Buffett's Japanese trading company bet is a model low-risk bet: he borrowed the entire $5 billion in yen at about 0.5% to buy stocks yielding about 8%, with no currency risk.
ideas.detail: Announced on his birthday, August 30, 2020, stakes over 5% in Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Marubeni, Sumitomo and Itochu; ~$400 million of dividends against $25 million of interest. Three years later dividends doubled, stocks doubled to quadrupled, the $5 billion became $12-13 billion and income is ~$800 million a year. The stocks were at multi-year lows and Japan was still 30-40% below its 1990 high.

ideas.idea: When a net-net basket has one winner and two laggards, do not rebalance mechanically; peel the onion to see if the laggards are structurally broken or melting ice cubes.
ideas.detail: Small amounts of capital can do well in these 'Mickey Mouse games' on the side, but always keep an eye out for compounders.

ideas.idea: The hack for finding compounders: list every brand you spend money on, find which are public, and ask why you chose them over competitors.
ideas.detail: Winning even a tiny part of a discerning consumer's spending is a huge accomplishment; as a consumer you already know much without the balance sheet. Peter Lynch advocated this. College students dropped landlines and cable first and used Facebook first, so Notre Dame students have a massive advantage over Buffett in Omaha, who changes nothing.

ideas.idea: Read Munger's 'Psychology of Human Misjudgment' every year; it distills 30-40 years of his stumbling into 30-plus models you can absorb in a day or two.
ideas.detail: Association tendency explains why Coke wants to be anywhere humans are happy (Olympics, World Cup, NFL, movie theaters) and uses celebrities; understanding the quirks in human wiring gives you a leg up on other humans.

ideas.idea: The reciprocation tendency has no calibration engine, so a small unsolicited gift can create a disproportionate sense of obligation.
ideas.detail: He sends prospective investors a physical package with a book and a Cross pen; only 1-2 in 100 return it, and for the rest 'the pen is equal to a few million dollars' minimum investment. Cialdini describes the same mechanism used by salespeople.

ideas.idea: Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so being a shameless cloner is a huge structural advantage.
ideas.detail: Nobody has cloned Chipotle's customizable assembly line (Baja Fresh never scaled; CAVA applied the concept to different food), McDonald's fries or the Egg McMuffin, even though there is room for two to four players in anything already proven.

ideas.idea: When a smart investor buys something you hate, study it to understand 'what drugs they were smoking'; Berkshire's and Einhorn's 2012 GM purchases led him to Fiat Chrysler.
ideas.detail: He hated autos (high capex, unions, consumer taste risk) but read Steve Rattner's 'Overhaul' and the 2009 UAW contract signed without changing a comma under threat of no bailout, and realized Detroit had become the best place to build cars again.

ideas.idea: Fiat Chrysler in 2012 had a $5-6 billion market cap on $135 billion of revenue, with the RAM and Jeep franchises each capable of over $5 billion a year in cash flow, plus 80% of Ferrari.
ideas.detail: He took a 10% position; Ferrari alone is now worth $50-60 billion (about $300 a share versus ~$15 a share of embedded value then) and the pieces became worth over $100 billion. Sergio Marchionne was the rock-star manager, and he sold too early in hindsight.

ideas.idea: Berkshire's recent purchase of homebuilders is likely because Lennar and others finally cloned the NVR model after 25 years of watching it outperform.
ideas.detail: NVR bought back about 85% of its stock, stopped dividends and became an 800-bagger in 25 years, 'a stupid homebuilder, not ChatGPT'; peers only copied it after they 'couldn't take it anymore'. Berkshire bought Lennar, D.R. Horton and others as a basket.

ideas.idea: Bridge and investing are both probabilistic games with no absolutes, which is why Buffett, Munger and many great investors play; taking up bridge makes you a better investor.
ideas.detail: Every investment has 'hair on it', e.g. what if Andy Jassy leaves Amazon or the FTC handcuffs it. He plays 5-6 hours a week, learns fastest playing with far better partners, and is now attending all three US national tournaments; Bridge Base costs about $99 a year.

ideas.idea: Learning accelerates when you play with people far better than you; a great teacher or coach matters.
ideas.detail: At 23 he was 'made minced meat of' by a frail 90-year-old couple at a bridge club, which forced him back to square one; he now plays with exceptional teachers as well as peers.

ideas.idea: Finding great charitable causes with high social returns is far harder than finding compounders, and Dakshana will cap out around $7-8 million a year of spending.
ideas.detail: Dakshana currently spends about $3 million a year and lucked into the IIT ecosystem. Homelessness in LA or San Francisco is a problem he is sure he would fail at. Like Buffett going from 50% a year on $1 million to barely beating the S&P on $600 billion, Dakshana will have to lower its bar as it scales.
